questions.question: A protractor is placed on an angle. The centre mark of the protractor sits exactly on the vertex, and one arm lies along the 0° mark of the inner scale. The other arm crosses the curved edge at a spot where the inner scale reads 50° and the outer scale reads 130°. What is the measure of the angle?
questions.explain: Read the scale that starts at 0° on the arm you lined up: that arm sits on 0° of the inner scale, so the answer is the inner reading, 50°. The usual trap is grabbing the other number at the same spot (130°) because it looks bigger.

questions.question: An angle is measured with a protractor. The centre mark is on the vertex and one arm lies along the 0° mark of the outer scale. The other arm crosses the curved edge where the outer scale reads 60° and the inner scale reads 120°. What is the measure of the angle?
questions.explain: Start counting from the 0° your arm is sitting on: it is on the outer scale, so keep reading the outer scale and you get 60°. Many students switch scales halfway and answer 120°, which is the reading for an arm that started at the other 0°.

questions.question: A student measures an angle. One arm lies on the 0° mark of the inner scale, and the other arm crosses the curved edge where the inner scale reads 115° and the outer scale reads 65°. Which name fits this angle?
options: An acute angle
A right angle
An obtuse angle
A reflex angle
questions.explain: The arm starts at 0° on the inner scale, so the angle is 115°, and any angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse. Reading 65° from the wrong scale would make you call it acute, so check your answer against 90° before naming it.

questions.question: Ravi wants to draw a 35° angle. He draws one ray, puts the centre mark of his protractor on the endpoint, and lines that ray up so it passes through the 0° mark of the inner scale. Where should he make his dot before drawing the second ray?
options: At 70° on the inner scale
At 35° on the outer scale
At 55° on the inner scale
At 35° on the inner scale
questions.explain: Your ray is on 0° of the inner scale, so count up the inner scale to 35° and mark there. Marking 35° on the outer scale puts the dot at the spot the inner scale calls 145°, and you end up drawing a wide angle instead of a sharp one.

questions.question: Jenna measures the angle her bike kickstand makes with the ground. She puts the centre mark on the vertex and lays the kickstand arm along the 0° mark of the outer scale. The ground arm crosses the curved edge where the outer scale reads 125° and the inner scale reads 55°. She first estimates that the angle is a bit wider than a square corner. What is the measure?
questions.explain: The arm sits on 0° of the outer scale, so read the outer scale: 125°, and that fits her estimate of 'wider than a right angle'. The 55° reading belongs to the other scale, and an estimate against 90° is the fastest way to catch that swap.

questions.question: Liam needs the reflex angle at the bottom of a playground slide. He measures the smaller angle first: one arm is on the 0° mark of the inner scale, and the other arm crosses where the inner scale reads 130° and the outer scale reads 50°. What is the reflex angle?
questions.explain: A protractor only reaches 180°, so measure the smaller angle (130° from the inner scale, since that is the scale the arm starts on) and subtract from a full turn: 360° − 130° = 230°. Reading 50° from the wrong scale would give 310°, which is far too big for the shape shown.

questions.question: Which of these is the correct way to set up a protractor before measuring an angle?
options: Line one arm up with the middle of the protractor, then read whichever number is larger.
Lay the straight edge anywhere along one arm and read where the other arm crosses.
Put the centre mark of the protractor exactly on the vertex and lay one arm along the 0° line.
Read both scales where the arm crosses and add the two numbers together.
questions.explain: The centre mark goes on the vertex and one arm goes on 0°, because the protractor counts degrees starting from that 0° line. Choosing the larger number instead of the scale that starts at your arm is the mistake that turns 60° into 120°.

questions.question: Mina measures the angle her hockey stick makes with the ice at practice in Langley. She puts the centre mark on the vertex and lays the stick arm along the 0° mark of the inner scale. The ice arm crosses the curved edge where the inner scale reads 70° and the outer scale reads 110°. She first estimates the angle is a bit narrower than a square corner. What is the measure?
questions.explain: The stick arm sits on 0° of the inner scale, so keep reading the inner scale: 70°, which fits her estimate of narrower than a right angle. The 110° reading belongs to the other scale, 90° is only the benchmark she estimated against, and 40° comes from subtracting one scale reading from the other instead of following one scale.

questions.question: Maya measures the angle of a ramp at the Burnaby skate park. She lays one arm along the 0° mark of the outer scale, and the other arm crosses where the outer scale reads 140° and the inner scale reads 40°. She writes 40°, but the ramp angle is clearly wider than a square corner. What should she write, and why?
options: 40°, because you always take the smaller reading on a protractor, since the bigger number is just the leftover part of the half turn.
220°, because she should subtract the 140° reading from 360°, since a wide angle is the part of the full turn that is left over.
90°, because a ramp always meets the ground at a right angle, so the protractor readings of 140° and 40° can both be ignored.
140°, because her arm starts at 0° on the outer scale, so she reads the outer scale, and 140° is more than 90°, matching a wide angle.
questions.explain: Follow the scale that begins at the 0° your arm is on, then check the answer against 90°: an angle that looks wider than a square corner must be more than 90°, so 140° is right. Taking the smaller number is exactly the habit that turns an obtuse angle into an acute one.

questions.question: Ella is drawing a kite for art class and needs a 105° angle. She draws a ray, puts the centre mark on its endpoint, and lines the ray up with the 0° mark of the outer scale. What should she do next?
options: Mark 105° on the outer scale, then check that the angle she drew looks a little wider than a square corner.
Mark 105° on the inner scale, because the inner numbers are the ones for drawing; the outer ones are for measuring.
Mark 75° on the outer scale, because 180° − 105° = 75° gives the number that pairs with 105° on a protractor.
Mark 105° on the inner scale, then check that the angle she drew looks a little smaller than a square corner.
questions.explain: Mark the degrees on the same scale your ray starts from — the outer one here — and then estimate against 90° to be sure the drawing matches. Marking 105° on the inner scale actually puts the dot where the outer scale says 75°, so the angle comes out too narrow.

questions.question: The classroom door swings open until only a narrow gap is left between the door and the wall. Emma measures that narrow angle: one arm is on the 0° mark of the inner scale, and the other arm crosses where the inner scale reads 35° and the outer scale reads 145°. What is the reflex angle the door has swung through on the other side?
questions.explain: First read the small angle from the scale that starts at 0° on the arm — 35° — then take it from a full turn: 360° − 35° = 325°. Using 145° from the other scale gives 215°, which is far too small for a door that is almost flat against the wall.

questions.question: Arjun wants to draw a 40° angle for his comic panel. He draws a ray, puts the centre mark on its endpoint, and lines the ray up with the 0° mark of the outer scale. Then he makes his dot at 40° on the inner scale — and the angle he draws looks much wider than a square corner. What went wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong with his method — 40° on the inner scale and 40° on the outer scale mark the very same spot, so the angle only looks wide because his ray is long.
He lined the ray up wrongly, because the ray must always start at 0° on the inner scale, never the outer, so every reading he takes from the outer scale is off.
His dot at 40° on the inner scale is where the outer scale — the one his ray starts on — reads 140°, so he drew 140°; the dot belongs at 40° on the outer scale.
He should have marked at 50° instead, because for drawing you use 90° − 40°, so the dot ends up on the correct side of the square corner and the angle looks right.
questions.explain: Mark the degrees on the scale whose 0° your ray starts from — the outer scale here — so the dot belongs at 40° on the outer scale. The spot labelled 40° on the inner scale is the same spot the outer scale calls 140°, which is exactly why his angle came out wide; either scale can be the starting scale, and 90° − 40° = 50° mixes in a rule that has nothing to do with protractor scales.
